title: Unsupervised Learning
summary: Unsupervised learning finds structure in data without labels. Clustering groups similar items, and dimensionality reduction compresses high-dimensional data (like embeddings) into fewer dimensions for visualization. These techniques are vital for exp
content:
# Unsupervised Learning ##### The cluster that was one document, 400 times A team in Kochi built a RAG chatbot over their company's internal wiki — about 12,000 pages, chunked into 61,000 pieces, embedded, and loaded into a vector store. Retrieval quality was poor in a strange way: certain unrelated questions all pulled back the same batch of chunks. Someone plotted the embeddings. They ran PCA down to two dimensions, made a scatter plot, and there it was — one enormously dense blob, far denser than anything else, sitting off to the side. They pulled 20 random points from the blob. All twenty were the company's email footer: *"This message and any attachments are confidential..."* The wiki export had included the footer on every page, and the chunker had faithfully turned it into 400 near-identical chunks. Those chunks were semantically close to nothing in particular, which meant they were mildly close to *everything*, and they were polluting every retrieval. The fix took ten minutes. **Finding the problem took one scatter plot.** That is what unsupervised learning gives you: structure in data you have no labels for. And for a GenAI engineer, whose primary raw material is a pile of unlabelled embeddings, it is not an academic topic — it is how you look at what you actually have. ##### What unsupervised learning is No labels. No right answers. Just data, and the question *what structure is in here?* Two main families: - **Clustering** — group similar items together. Which of these customers behave alike? Which of these support tickets are about the same issue? - **Dimensionality reduction** — compress many dimensions into few, keeping as much structure as possible. Take 1,536-dimensional embeddings down to 2 so you can plot them. Plus a close cousin, **anomaly detection**: find the points that fit no pattern. Because there is no ground truth, **evaluation is genuinely harder**. There is no accuracy to compute. You use internal measures (how tight are the clusters?), stability checks (do you get the same clusters on a different sample?), and — most importantly — human judgement. A clustering is good if it is *useful*, and you find that out by looking. ##### K-Means clustering K-Means partitions data into `k` groups by finding `k` centre points and assigning each item to its nearest one. The algorithm alternates two steps until nothing changes: 1. **Assign** — each point joins the cluster of its nearest centroid. 2. **Update** — each centroid moves to the mean of its assigned points. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Pick k random
starting centroids"] --> B["Assign each point
to nearest centroid"] B --> C["Move each centroid to
the mean of its points"] C --> D{"Did anything
move?"} D -->|Yes| B D -->|No| E["Converged:
final clusters"] ``` ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.cluster import KMeans from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score rng = np.random.default_rng(42) n = 600 customers = np.column_stack([ rng.choice([2, 9, 22], n, p=[.45, .35, .20]) + rng.normal(0, 1.4, n), # orders/month rng.choice([450, 1800, 6200], n, p=[.45, .35, .20]) + rng.normal(0, 220, n), # ₹ spend rng.uniform(1, 36, n), # tenure months ]) pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=42)) labels = pipe.fit_predict(customers) km = pipe.named_steps["kmeans"] print("cluster sizes:", np.bincount(labels)) print("inertia:", round(km.inertia_, 1)) print("silhouette:", round(silhouette_score( pipe.named_steps["standardscaler"].transform(customers), labels), 3)) ``` **Scaling is mandatory.** K-Means uses Euclidean distance, and here `spend` runs to 6,200 while `orders` runs to 22. Without scaling, spend is the only feature that matters and the other two are decoration. Two other essentials. **`n_init=10`** runs the algorithm ten times from different random starts and keeps the best, because K-Means can converge to a poor local optimum depending on where the centroids begin. And **`random_state`** makes it reproducible. **What K-Means assumes**, and therefore where it fails: it looks for roughly spherical, similarly-sized clusters. Give it two crescent moons or one huge cluster next to a tiny one, and it will split them wrongly. It also forces every point into some cluster — there is no "none of the above." ##### Choosing the number of clusters `k` is your decision, and there is no formula that produces the right answer. Two standard tools: **The elbow method** — plot inertia (total within-cluster squared distance) against `k`. Inertia always falls as `k` rises, so you look for the bend where extra clusters stop buying much. **Silhouette score** — for each point, compare its distance to its own cluster against its distance to the nearest other cluster. Ranges from −1 to +1. Above 0.5 is decent structure; near 0 means clusters overlap; negative means points are in the wrong cluster. ```python from sklearn.cluster import KMeans from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score import matplotlib.pyplot as plt X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(customers) ks = range(2, 11) inertias, silhouettes = [], [] for k in ks: km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(X) inertias.append(km.inertia_) silhouettes.append(silhouette_score(X, km.labels_)) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4)) axes[0].plot(ks, inertias, "o-") axes[0].set_xlabel("k"); axes[0].set_ylabel("Inertia") axes[0].set_title("Elbow: look for the bend", loc="left") axes[1].plot(ks, silhouettes, "o-", color="#c44e52") axes[1].set_xlabel("k"); axes[1].set_ylabel("Silhouette") axes[1].set_title("Silhouette: higher is better", loc="left") fig.tight_layout() best_k = ks[int(np.argmax(silhouettes))] print("best k by silhouette:", best_k) ``` **But the real test is interpretability.** If `k=7` scores marginally better and `k=3` gives you three segments the business can name and act on — "occasional buyers," "regulars," "high-value loyalists" — pick 3. Clusters nobody can describe are clusters nobody will use. Always profile your clusters afterwards: ```python import pandas as pd df = pd.DataFrame(customers, columns=["orders", "spend", "tenure"]) df["cluster"] = labels print(df.groupby("cluster").agg(["mean", "count"]).round(1)) ``` ##### Hierarchical clustering Instead of choosing `k` up front, hierarchical clustering builds a tree. Agglomerative (bottom-up) starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the closest pair until one cluster remains. ```python from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, linkage, fcluster Z = linkage(X[:80], method="ward") # ward minimises within-cluster variance fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4)) dendrogram(Z, ax=ax, truncate_mode="level", p=5, no_labels=True) ax.set_title("Dendrogram — cut at a height to choose clusters", loc="left") ax.set_ylabel("Merge distance") labels_h = fcluster(Z, t=3, criterion="maxclust") ``` The **dendrogram** shows the whole merge history, and you choose `k` afterwards by cutting the tree at a height. Long vertical lines before a merge mean those groups were quite different — a natural place to cut. Linkage methods change the result: `ward` (minimise variance, gives compact clusters), `average`, `complete` (compact, outlier-sensitive), `single` (can produce long chains). `ward` is the sensible default. Hierarchical clustering is $O(n^2)$ or worse in memory, so it is practical up to a few thousand points. Use it for exploring structure; use K-Means or DBSCAN at scale. ##### PCA PCA finds the directions along which your data varies most, and lets you keep only the top few. Day 6 gave you the mechanism — eigenvectors of the covariance matrix. Here is what it means practically. ```python from sklearn.decomposition import PCA embeddings = rng.standard_normal((2000, 384)) # stand-in for real embeddings pca = PCA(n_components=50, random_state=42) reduced = pca.fit_transform(embeddings) print("explained variance by top 2:", pca.explained_variance_ratio_[:2].round(3)) print("cumulative by 50 comps:", pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum().round(3)) # How many components to keep 95% of the variance? pca_full = PCA().fit(embeddings) cum = np.cumsum(pca_full.explained_variance_ratio_) print("components for 95%:", np.argmax(cum >= 0.95) + 1) ``` Key properties: - **PCA is linear.** It finds straight-line directions of variance. Curved structure is invisible to it. - **Centre your data first** — scikit-learn does this automatically; if you implement it yourself, do not forget. - **Scale features first** when they are on different units, or the largest-range feature dominates every component. - **`explained_variance_ratio_`** tells you how much information each component retains, so you can decide how many to keep honestly. - **It is invertible** — `pca.inverse_transform()` reconstructs an approximation, which is what makes PCA useful for compression and denoising. For embeddings specifically, PCA down to 50–100 dimensions before clustering often *improves* results, because it strips noise and mitigates the curse of dimensionality. ##### t-SNE and UMAP PCA is great for compression but often poor for visualisation, because forcing 384 dimensions onto a straight-line plane crushes local structure. t-SNE and UMAP are non-linear methods built specifically for making 2-D pictures. **t-SNE** (van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008) converts distances into probabilities and arranges points in 2-D so those probabilities match. It preserves **local** neighbourhoods beautifully. ```python from sklearn.manifold import TSNE # Standard practice: PCA first for speed and noise reduction, then t-SNE pre = PCA(n_components=50, random_state=42).fit_transform(embeddings) tsne = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, init="pca", learning_rate="auto", random_state=42) coords = tsne.fit_transform(pre) plt.figure(figsize=(7, 6)) plt.scatter(coords[:, 0], coords[:, 1], s=6, alpha=0.6) plt.title("Embedding space — look for suspicious dense blobs", loc="left") ``` **UMAP** does something similar with a different mathematical foundation. It is much faster, scales to millions of points, preserves more global structure, and — crucially — can transform new points without refitting. | | PCA | t-SNE | UMAP | |---|---|---|---| | Type | Linear | Non-linear | Non-linear | | Speed | Very fast | Slow | Fast | | Preserves | Global variance | Local neighbourhoods | Local + some global | | Deterministic | Yes | No (seed it) | No (seed it) | | Transform new points | Yes | No | Yes | | Best for | Compression, preprocessing | Small-data visualisation | Large-data visualisation | **Three warnings about t-SNE that trip up everyone.** Cluster *sizes* in a t-SNE plot are meaningless — a tight blob is not necessarily a tight cluster. *Distances between* clusters are also mostly meaningless. And the `perplexity` parameter (roughly, how many neighbours to consider, typically 5–50) changes the picture substantially, so try several before drawing conclusions. Use t-SNE and UMAP to **generate hypotheses**, then verify them in the original space — exactly what the Kochi team did when they pulled 20 real chunks out of that blob. ##### Anomaly detection Anomalies are points that do not fit the pattern. For a GenAI pipeline: corrupted documents, near-duplicate spam, embeddings from a failed API call that came back as all zeros. ```python from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor iso = IsolationForest(contamination=0.02, random_state=42) flags = iso.fit_predict(X) # -1 = anomaly, 1 = normal print("anomalies found:", (flags == -1).sum()) lof = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20, contamination=0.02) flags_lof = lof.fit_predict(X) ``` **Isolation Forest** works on a clever insight: anomalies are easier to isolate with random splits, because they sit alone. It is fast and works well in high dimensions. **Local Outlier Factor** compares each point's local density to its neighbours', catching anomalies that are only unusual *relative to their region*. A simpler check worth running on every embedding pipeline: ```python norms = np.linalg.norm(embeddings, axis=1) print("zero-norm vectors:", (norms < 1e-6).sum()) # failed API calls ``` ##### Common mistakes - **Not scaling before K-Means or PCA**, so one large-range feature decides everything. - **`n_init=1`**, leaving you at the mercy of a bad random start. - **Choosing `k` purely by silhouette** without checking whether the clusters mean anything. - **Reading cluster sizes or inter-cluster distances off a t-SNE plot.** Both are artifacts. - **A single perplexity setting**, then treating the resulting picture as truth. - **Running t-SNE on raw 1,536-dim embeddings** — do PCA to ~50 first; it is faster and cleaner. - **Forgetting to centre data before manual PCA**, making the first component point at the mean. - **Treating clusters as ground truth.** They are a hypothesis to inspect, not a label. - **Assuming anomalies are errors.** Sometimes the outlier is your most interesting data point. - **Never actually looking at cluster members.** Pull ten real examples from each cluster and read them — that is where the Kochi footer was found. ##### Hands-on: look at your embeddings Your practical task is K-Means with the elbow method and PCA visualisation. Do all three steps as one loop: cluster, plot the elbow and silhouette, then project to 2-D with PCA and colour by cluster label. If the clusters overlap heavily in the PCA plot, that is informative — it may mean the structure is non-linear, which is precisely when you reach for UMAP. The mini project builds a customer-segmentation tool with PCA visualisation. Go beyond the plot: after clustering, produce a profile table showing each cluster's mean on every feature plus its size, and then *name* each segment in plain language. "Cluster 2: 118 customers, 22 orders/month, ₹6,200 spend, 28 months tenure — call these Loyal High-Value." A segmentation you can name is a segmentation the business can act on. The assignment compares PCA and t-SNE on high-dimensional data. Run both on the same dataset and put the plots side by side. You will typically see PCA give a diffuse cloud with mild structure while t-SNE gives crisp separated islands. Then write the honest comparison: t-SNE's picture is prettier and better for spotting groups, but PCA's axes mean something, PCA is deterministic, and only PCA can project a new unseen point. Knowing when the prettier plot is the wrong tool is the actual skill. ##### Key takeaways - **Unsupervised learning finds structure without labels** — and for a GenAI engineer, whose data is a pile of unlabelled embeddings, it is how you inspect what you actually have. - **K-Means needs scaled features, `n_init` above 1, and a `k` you choose** using the elbow and silhouette *plus* whether the clusters are nameable. - **PCA is linear, fast, deterministic, and invertible** — use it for compression, preprocessing, and honest variance accounting. - **t-SNE and UMAP make better pictures but lie about cluster sizes and distances**; use them to form hypotheses, then verify in the original space. - **Always pull real examples out of each cluster and read them.** One scatter plot and twenty sampled chunks is what found the 400 duplicated email footers.
practical_task_reference: Apply K-Means to a dataset, choose k with the elbow method, and visualize clusters with PCA.
mini_project_reference: Build a customer-segmentation tool that clusters users and visualizes segments in 2D using PCA.
assignment_reference: Compare PCA and t-SNE on a high-dimensional dataset and discuss when each is appropriate.
